Lake District Passes: England's Most Thrilling Roads

The Lake District contains England's steepest, most challenging, and most rewarding motorcycle roads. These passes climb through some of the country's finest scenery, with gradients that rival Alpine cols. Here's everything you need to know before tackling them on two wheels.

Hardknott Pass

Hardknott Pass is England's steepest road with gradients reaching 33%. The narrow, unfenced road climbs from Eskdale to the summit at 393 metres, with tight hairpin bends and sheer drops. It's a genuine test of clutch control and nerve. The Roman fort at the summit (Mediobogdum) is worth a stop — the views across the Eskdale valley are spectacular.

  • Gradient: Up to 33%
  • Surface: Variable, some loose gravel on bends
  • Best direction: West to east (Eskdale to Wrynose)
  • Avoid: Bank holiday weekends, when traffic queues form

Wrynose Pass

Often paired with Hardknott, Wrynose Pass connects the Duddon Valley with Little Langdale. It's slightly less extreme than Hardknott but still features 25% gradients and tight bends. The combination of both passes is one of England's greatest motorcycle adventures — roughly 15 miles of continuous mountain riding.

Kirkstone Pass

The Kirkstone Pass is the Lake District's most accessible mountain road. The A592 climbs to 454 metres between Ambleside and Patterdale, with the Kirkstone Pass Inn at the summit — one of England's highest pubs. The Struggle, the steep section from Ambleside, earns its name with several acute hairpins.

Ride the passes midweek and early in the morning for the best experience. By mid-morning in summer, tourist traffic makes progress painfully slow.

Honister Pass

The B5289 over Honister connects Buttermere with Borrowdale. The pass reaches 356 metres and features 25% gradients on the Borrowdale side. The slate mine at the summit offers tours, and the views down into both valleys are quintessentially Lakeland. This pass is best combined with the loop through Buttermere and over Newlands Pass for a complete circuit.

Newlands Pass and Others

The Newlands Pass is a hidden gem — quieter than the more famous passes and equally beautiful. The road climbs from Braithwaite to Buttermere through a hanging valley with views of Derwentwater. Other notable climbs include the Whinlatter Pass (England's only mountain forest) and the Dunmail Raise on the A591.

Practical Tips

Many Lake District passes are single-track with passing places. Give way to uphill traffic and pull into passing places on your left. The road surfaces can be rough with loose gravel, especially after rain. First gear and careful clutch control are essential on the steepest sections. Avoid riding the passes in wet conditions if you're inexperienced — the gradients combined with wet tarmac demand respect. keyTakeaways: Hardknott Pass is England's steepest road at up to 33%, climbing from Eskdale to 393 metres.
Wrynose Pass pairs with Hardknott for roughly 15 miles of continuous mountain riding at up to 25%.
Kirkstone Pass is the most accessible at 454 metres, home to one of England's highest pubs.
Honister and Newlands passes offer quieter 25% climbs linking Buttermere with Borrowdale and Braithwaite.
Many passes are single-track with passing places; give way to uphill traffic and avoid wet conditions if inexperienced.

faq.q: Which is the steepest Lake District pass?
faq.a: Hardknott Pass is England's steepest road, with gradients reaching 33%. The narrow, unfenced road climbs from Eskdale to a summit at 393 metres with tight hairpins and sheer drops, demanding good clutch control and steady nerve. The Roman fort at the top rewards the effort with spectacular views.

faq.q: What is the best direction to ride Hardknott?
faq.a: Ride west to east, from Eskdale over Hardknott and on to Wrynose. Combining the two passes gives roughly 15 miles of continuous mountain riding, one of England's greatest motorcycle adventures. Avoid bank holiday weekends when traffic queues form on the narrow single-track sections.

faq.q: Are the passes safe for less experienced riders?
faq.a: They demand respect. Many are single-track with passing places, surfaces can be rough with loose gravel especially after rain, and the steepest sections need first gear and careful clutch control. If you are inexperienced, avoid riding the passes in the wet, as gradients plus wet tarmac are unforgiving.

faq.q: When is the best time to ride the Lake District passes?
faq.a: Ride midweek and early in the morning for the best experience. By mid-morning in summer, tourist traffic makes progress painfully slow on these narrow roads. Late spring and early autumn offer the ideal balance of daylight, drier tarmac and quieter conditions on the passes.
